title: On Schooling, AI, and Luxury Beliefs
author: Birmingham Teacher
summary: A Birmingham secondary-school leader writes from a boots-on-the-ground perspective to interrogate the cultural enthusiasm for AI-driven schooling, specifically the Alpha School model (two hours of AI-mediated academics per day, the rest enrichment and life-skills workshops). The author acknowledges genuine applications of AI in education -- particularly Carl Hendrick's argument about AI's potential in fine-grained formative assessment -- but argues these gains cannot justify dismantling the human architecture of schooling: physical presence, teacher-student relationships, and a rich curriculum through which children access something larger than themselves. The core argument applies Rob Henderson's 'luxury beliefs' framework to AI-heavy education: wealthy families can adopt AI-heavy models from a position of insulation ($10,000--$75,000/year tuition), while regular schools bear the indirect costs -- losing top graduates to 'Guide' roles, normalizing unverified outcomes. The author identifies motivation as the structural problem AI-based schooling cannot solve: children must practise things they do not want to practise, and the transition from external to internal motivators requires human scaffolding that adaptive software has not been shown to provide. The article defends traditional schooling not from technophobia but from a clear account of what schooling is actually for: not efficient content mastery but the induction of children into Michael Oakeshott's 'conversation of mankind,' with a teacher who is present, who cares, and who makes every student feel they matter.
points: The Alpha School model optimizes for academic efficiency -- 'crush academics in 2 hours' -- at the expense of the curriculum's real function: inducting children into a shared intellectual inheritance through slow, effortful, relational engagement with genuinely difficult material, including whole books.

Rob Henderson's luxury beliefs framework applies here: wealthy families adopt AI-heavy schooling from a position of insulation and confer status on the model, while the indirect costs -- top graduates rerouted from teaching, unverified outcomes normalized -- fall on communities that cannot afford to experiment.

Greg Ashman's structural objection: Alpha School's claimed outcomes have not been independently verified, and its student population is self-selected (parents who chose and paid for it) -- making any performance comparison with traditional schools methodologically meaningless.

The motivational problem reveals AI-based learning's structural limits: children must practise things they do not want to practise, and the external-to-internal motivational transition requires human scaffolding that no adaptive software has been shown to reliably provide.
quotes: In our school communities, kids need to feel they matter. That they are valuable and valued. That we want them to be there to learn because it's important, interesting stuff. There in person, in front of us, detached from a screen. That every child in a class is heard. That they are welcome and important and safe.

The ever-creeping use of AI as a tool by which students think they 'learn' something is very concerning. For many of them, ChatGPT is a go-to for finding stuff, and thinking they know it. But they're not learning it, and don't know it, and are certainly not questioning it.

Isn't there something hauntingly depressing in this vision of schooling? Something hollowed out and empty and sad? Where is the curriculum that helps children know and argue and challenge and build? Where is the design of a beautiful curriculum so that our children can, in Michael Oakeshott's words, enter into the conversation of mankind?

Rob Henderson argues that affluent people promote luxury beliefs because they know that the adoption of those beliefs will cost them less than others. He argues that luxury beliefs confer status on the upper class... while inflicting costs on the lower classes.

It is this problem that education needs to address and it is a hard problem. We might assume that engaging visuals or a pseudo-intelligent computer program would help children over the motivational hump, but history tells us otherwise. It takes far more -- external motivators that gradually transition to internal motivators as capabilities incrementally increase. Children need to practise things they don't really want to practise.

I remember sitting in that class thinking I had never, ever before felt anything so viscerally when reading a text. That feeling that shook and broke the voice of my 17-year-old self as I read made me feel something bigger than I had ever thought possible: it took me beyond the perimeter of my own life into a different time, space, person and being. It gave me the power of thought that I didn't know I was capable of. And that was beautiful, and enabling, and empowering.
